bridge.A town on Goose Flats: The hills were full of tents and shovels now. And all those people needed somewhere to live. Where would you have pitched your tent?
bridge.Down in the silver mines: Above ground, you could watch the town growing fast. But the real reason for all of it lay deep beneath your feet.
bridge.Evenings on Allen Street: When the shift whistle blew and the miners climbed back into the daylight, the town came alive. Shall we follow them into town?
bridge.Nellie Cashman: Among the crowds on those busy streets, you'd soon notice a few people that everyone in town seemed to know.
bridge.George Parsons and his diary: Nellie fed the town. Another newcomer quietly wrote it all down, and that's lucky for you and me.
bridge.Newspapers and photographs: Parsons kept his diary for himself. But Tombstone also had people who recorded its days for everyone to read and see. Have you ever wondered where those old pictures came from?
bridge.The Earp brothers and Doc Holliday: Some of the people in those photographs would one day become far more famous than they ever expected. You probably know a few of their names already.
bridge.Ranches, cowboys and lawmen: Beyond the edge of town, the land opened out into wide, quiet valleys. Ride out there with me, and you'll see that not everyone saw things the same way.
bridge.Two days in October: Through the long summer, old quarrels simmered quietly. Then, in late October, they came to the surface. Let's walk through those two days slowly and gently.
bridge.Thirty seconds, and after: What happened next has been told and retold for more than a hundred years. You might think it went on for a long time. In real life, it was over very quickly.
bridge.What became of them: Slowly, life in Tombstone went back to its ordinary rhythm. But the town itself was about to change. Do you wonder what happened to everyone?
bridge.Tombstone today: The people of those years are long gone now. Yet the town they knew is still there, on its high desert mesa, and you can still walk its streets.
